predecessors.name: Seleucid Empire
predecessors.text: 'The Kingdom of Gordyene emerged from the declining Seleucid Empire'; 'From 189 to 90 BCE, it enjoyed a period of independence'

successors.name: Roman Empire
successors.text: Corduene among the satrapies east of the Tigris ceded to Rome by the Peace of Nisibis in 299; the page says it was 'conquered again by Diocletian'

ledger.x: 189 BC: Gordyene is independent of the Seleucids.
By 95 BC: Gordyene a Parthian vassal.
88-85 BC: Tigranes the Great takes Gordyene from Parthia.
88-85 BC: Gordyene an Armenian vassal of Tigranes ('the Submission of Gordyene under its prince', Corduene page; 'Gordyene belonged to...
67 BC: Parthia attacks Gordyene while Tigranes holds it.
65 BC (bridged): the dispute goes to Pompey.
65 BC (bridged): the occupation passes into Pompey's settlement.
27 BC (bridged): the republic's protection ends with the republic.
Late 1st century BC: Gordyene an Adiabenian dependency ('starting at least with the rule of Monobazos I (late 1st-century BCE), Gordyene became an Adiabenian dependency').

116 (bridged): the dependency ends with Adiabene's annexation by Trajan, as in the kingdom-of-adiabene dossier; the Corduene page (re-opened) says nothing about Adiabene, and Manisarus 'sided with the Romans' about 115.
240 (bridged): Gordyene a Sasanian vassal so that the 299 cession has a giver.
299: the Sasanian relation ends with the cession of Corduene to Rome (see the loss event).
299: the Kingdom of Gordyene ends in the Roman Empire.

wars.name: Third Mithridatic War
wars.outcome: Zarbienus of Corduene killed by Tigranes in 69 BC after plotting revolt; Lucullus took over the region; Pompey 'gave protection to the newly acquired territory of Gordyene'; the Corduene dispute between Tigranes and Phraates went to Pompey (66/65 BC).

wars.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign
wars.outcome: '~ 115 AD: He took control over parts of Armenia and Mesopotamia, in the time of Trajan'; Manisarus sided with the Romans.

wars.name: Roman-Sasanian War of 296-299
wars.outcome: Roman victory; the Peace of Nisibis (299) ceded five satrapies east of the Tigris, Corduene among them in the page's lists.

certainty.note: The page gives the Tigris left bank and Bohtan, not a boundary.
The Peace of Nisibis made the Tigris the border between the empires.
